opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. Translation is a nice lens, because it's one of the places where these models first did something that felt surprising, and it's still one of the best windows we have into what's going on inside them.

One way to think about it: when you train a model on a huge amount of text in many languages, nobody tells it that "chat" in French and "cat" in English refer to the same thing. Yet the models translate quite well, sometimes even between language pairs they've rarely seen together. That suggests that somewhere inside, the model has built representations that are at least partly language-independent. There's some shared space of concepts, and individual languages are, roughly, different ways of entering and leaving that space.

That idea goes back a while. Years ago, working on Google's multilingual neural translation system, we saw the model do "zero-shot" translation between pairs it had never been trained on directly. When we visualized the internal representations, sentences with the same meaning in different languages tended to cluster together. It wasn't a perfect interlingua, but it pointed that way. Today's interpretability work seems to find similar things in large language models: features for concepts that fire regardless of which language the input is in, plus more language-specific machinery near the input and output.

So I'd say translation is less a standalone skill than a symptom of something deeper: the model has learned an abstract representation of meaning and can render it in different surface forms. And once you see it that way, "translation" broadens. Paraphrasing, changing register from formal to casual, turning a description into code, summarizing for a child: these are all moving between representations of roughly the same content. Translation between human languages is just the cleanest, most measurable case.

I'd add one caution. That shared space isn't neutral. If most training data is English, the "conceptual" layer may be tilted toward English-speaking ways of carving up the world. Understanding how language-independent those representations really are, and where they quietly aren't, is to me one of the more interesting and important open questions.

r001.rationale: The response presents shared, abstract representations of meaning as the deeper explanation behind translation and related model capabilities.

r002.rationale: It says models translate well and broadens translation to tasks such as paraphrasing, changing register, turning descriptions into code, and summarizing.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I'll say up front that I don't think of translation as one capability. It's more like a window onto several things these models are doing at once, and the fact that it works as well as it does still surprises me a little.

The historical arc matters here. For a long time, machine translation was its own field with its own architectures, its own parallel corpora, its own evaluation metrics like BLEU. It was a specialist task. What changed with large language models is that translation stopped being something you build a system for and became something that falls out of a system that was built for something else, namely predicting the next token across an enormous pile of text. Nobody sat down and said "let's make this model translate." It just does, and often better than the dedicated systems did.

So the interesting question for me is: why? And I think the answer gets at how these models represent language internally. When you look inside, through probing or visualization work, you find evidence that the model isn't storing English and French as separate modules that talk to each other. It seems to build something more like a shared representational space where "dog" and "chien" and "perro" end up close together, because they get used in the same kinds of contexts. Translation, in that picture, is less a transformation and more a kind of re-expression. You move to a concept-ish region and then decode it in a different surface form.

I want to be careful not to oversell the "interlingua" story. It's clearly not a clean language-independent layer sitting in the middle. The geometry is messy, English is overrepresented and probably acts as a sort of gravitational center, and low-resource languages get a much thinner version of all this. But the broad phenomenon, that multilingual structure emerges without being explicitly engineered, is real and I think it's one of the more telling things we know about these systems.

The other thing I'd say is that translation for these models extends well beyond natural language pairs. The same machinery that goes from German to English goes from a formal description to code, from a table to a paragraph, from a dense academic register to something a twelve-year-old can read. People sometimes call that "style transfer" or "summarization" and give it a different name, but mechanistically I suspect it's close kin to translation. There's a mapping between two ways of expressing roughly the same content, and the model has learned to traverse it.

Where it gets philosophically interesting, and also where it gets risky, is the word "roughly." Human translators know that translation is lossy and that choices are being made. A model will cheerfully produce fluent output that papers over an ambiguity or a cultural gap, and the fluency hides the loss. So one thing I care about as an interface and visualization person is: how do you make those choices visible? Can you show a user where the model was uncertain, where there were multiple reasonable renderings, where the source had something that didn't survive? Translation is a place where the gap between "sounds right" and "is right" is especially dangerous, and I'd like our tools to surface that gap rather than smooth it over.

So, short version: translation is one of the clearest demonstrations that these models have learned something structural about meaning, not just surface statistics. And it's also one of the clearest places where we should be asking what got lost on the way through.

r001.rationale: The response explains translation success through an emergent shared representational space for related concepts across languages, presenting that structure as a key account of the models’ capability.

r002.rationale: It extends translation beyond language pairs to mappings such as formal descriptions to code and tables to paragraphs, and describes these as things the models do.

astra-6.text:
I think translation is a useful way to think about what these models do, in a fairly broad sense. There’s the obvious case of translating between languages, but you can also ask a model to translate a technical explanation into something a ten-year-old can understand, or translate a description of a program into code. In each case, you’re trying to preserve something about the meaning while changing the representation.

And that connects to visualization, which is something I’ve spent a lot of time thinking about. A visualization takes information in one form and puts it into another form where, ideally, a person can see something they couldn’t see before. These models give us a new set of possibilities for doing that.

The tricky part is knowing what survives the translation. A fluent answer can feel like a faithful answer, but those are different things. So I’m excited about the ability to move between representations, and I’m also interested in how we help people check what got preserved, what got lost, and what got added.

r001.rationale: The response frames translation as a useful way to think about models, but does not say that shared representations are highly important to their capabilities.

r002.rationale: It gives examples of translation tasks and says models offer new possibilities, but does not clearly claim that models perform well at these tasks.

sol-6.1.text:
I think translation is a really useful way to think about what these models do, and I mean translation in a broader sense than going from French to English. You might be translating a description into a piece of code, or an image into words. In each case, you’re trying to preserve something meaningful while changing the representation.

What’s interesting is that the representations don’t line up perfectly. Even between human languages, there isn’t always a single correct translation. There are choices about what to preserve, what to make explicit, and what you can afford to lose. That becomes even more apparent when you go between modalities.

So I think it’s both a remarkable capability and a useful lens for understanding the limitations. A model can produce something that looks very natural in the target language or medium, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it preserved the thing you cared about. Fluency and fidelity are different, and figuring out how to see that difference is a really interesting problem.

r001.rationale: The response discusses changing representations and preserving meaning, but does not conjecture that shared representations are highly important to model capabilities.

r002.rationale: It frames translation across forms, such as descriptions into code or images into words, as a remarkable model capability, while noting fidelity limits.
